Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks

Youqing Fang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Zhouqi Hua Affiliation: Fudan University    Yinhao Tang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Yuzhe Gu Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University    Lingkai Kong Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University   
Bin Liu Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Weiming Zhang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Kai Chen Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Yanan Sun    Wenwei Zhang
Abstract

Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem–solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition–proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

Project page: https://tome-math.github.io/

11footnotetext: Equal contribution, †Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Mathematical reasoning in large language models has advanced rapidly, driven in part by improvements in training data and in part by advances in reasoning-time computation [28, 38, 21, 13, 37, 4, 27, 42, 10, 29, 15, 1, 2]. On the data side, recent efforts have expanded mathematical supervision to millions of QA pairs (i.e., Question-Answer pairs) and in doing so have revealed that properties such as question diversity, solution format, and teacher-model quality significantly shape downstream performance [39, 40, 31, 18]. These findings suggest a broader principle: The value of mathematical supervision is not determined by the number of training examples alone, but also by how those examples are constructed and organized.

Despite this, the dominant paradigm for mathematical supervision remains the isolated problem–solution pair. Whether the original knowledge comes from competition archives, grade-school word problems, web exercises, or synthetic augmentation, the resulting training data typically takes the uniform shape of problem→solution\text{problem}\to\text{solution} [7, 14, 39]. This representation is convenient to scale, but it does not explicitly leverage the organizational structure that many source materials already possess.

Mathematical textbooks are a notable case in point. A textbook is not merely a collection of solved problems, but a carefully structured body of knowledge. Definitions introduce core concepts, lemmas and theorems develop them, proofs establish their validity, and exercises reinforce understanding. These elements are organized within a chapter hierarchy that reflects prerequisite relations, conceptual dependencies, and pedagogical progression. Prior work has explored textbooks as a source of mathematical pretraining data, problem–solution pairs, and proof supervision [33, 30, 35, 3, 16, 19, 41]. However, textbooks are often treated primarily as sources of mathematical content, leaving their native structure underexplored. In particular, it remains unclear how to scale natural-language proof supervision while preserving chapter order, proposition dependencies, source locations, and exercises in a unified framework.

To address this gap, we introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale proof-supervision resource constructed from 2,118 mathematics textbooks. Central to TOME-Math is the notion of structured mathematical supervision, which preserves structure at three levels. First, hierarchical structure retains the native organization of textbooks, including chapters, propositions, and their ordering. Second, dependency structure connects theorem-level proof questions with the intermediate proof obligations derived from gaps in their proofs. Third, curriculum structure organizes supervision according to textbook order and proof granularity, enabling controlled training over related examples rather than independent QA pairs. Following these principles, TOME-Math contains 380,292 proof-oriented QA pairs spanning 29 mathematical subjects. Figure 1 provides an overview of the construction and organization of the resulting corpus.

We further validate the effectiveness of TOME-Math through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a 30B base model [37]. Its retained structure enables controlled studies of how the organization of supervision affects mathematical reasoning. Rather than treating scale as the only variable, TOME-Math allows us to examine the roles of retrieval structure, curriculum order, and source coverage under controlled settings. Empirically, TOME-Math SFT improves the six-benchmark average from 29.17% to 45.83%, while further experiments show consistent benefits from structure-guided retrieval, textbook-aligned curricula, and broader source coverage. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce TOME-Math, a large-scale proof-supervision resource constructed from 2,118 mathematics textbooks. Through a structure-preserving pipeline, it produces 380,292 Concept and Gap QA records while retaining chapter progression, proposition–proof links, dependency references, source provenance, and a separate inventory of textbook-authored exercises.

  • •

    We demonstrate the overall effectiveness of TOME-Math through full-corpus fine-tuning. On book-held-out textbook exercises and established public benchmarks, TOME-Math achieves the best performance on five of six evaluations, improving the unweighted six-benchmark mean from 29.17% to 45.83% over the base model and outperforming all three public instruction-data baselines in aggregate.

  • •

    We systematically investigate how textbook structure contributes to mathematical reasoning at inference and training time. Structure-guided retrieval improves proof-generation pass@1 from 13.25% to 17.38% under a matched context budget; across six subjects and three data scales, forward textbook curricula consistently outperform shuffled and reverse schedules; and broader source coverage yields further gains under a fixed training-token budget.
